content: During the 1950s and 1960s, the Soviet Union conducted numerous experiments using dogs to assess the feasibility of human spaceflight. These experiments involved both sub-orbital and orbital missions. At least 57 dogs were used in these missions, though the actual number of individual dogs was smaller, as some participated in multiple flights. Most of the dogs survived, with fatalities primarily resulting from technical failures. Training Dogs were chosen for these experiments because scientists believed they were better suited to endure prolonged periods of inactivity compared to other animals. Stray dogs were specifically selected over domesticated ones, as they were thought to be more resilient to the extreme stresses of space travel. Female dogs were preferred due to their temperament and because the suits designed to collect urine and feces were tailored for females. The training regimen for these dogs was rigorous. It included confinement in small boxes for 15–20 days at a time, wearing space suits, standing still for extended periods, and being placed in simulators that mimicked the conditions of rocket launches. They were also subjected to centrifuge rides to simulate the high acceleration of a rocket launch and were gradually confined to smaller cages to prepare them for the limited space within the capsules. Dogs that flew in orbit were fed a jelly-like protein-rich food designed to aid digestion during long periods of inactivity. Despite these measures, over 60% of the dogs experienced constipation and gallbladder stones upon their return. Sub-Orbital Flights Several dogs participated in high-altitude flights on R-1 series geophysical rockets between 1951 and 1952. Dezik and Tsygan: On July 22, 1951, Dezik and Tsygan became the first dogs to make a sub-orbital flight, reaching an altitude of 100 km. Both were recovered unharmed. Tsygan was later adopted as a pet by Soviet physicist Anatoli Blagonravov. Dezik flew again in September 1951 with a dog named Lisa, but neither survived. Lisa and Ryzhik: On June 2, 1954, Lisa and Ryzhik reached an altitude of 100 km. Smelaya and Malyshka: Smelaya, whose name means Bold or Courageous, was scheduled for a flight in September but ran away the day before the launch. She was found the next day and successfully flew with Malyshka (Little One). Bolik and ZIB: Bolik ran away days before her flight in September 1951. An untrained stray dog, later named ZIB (an acronym for Substitute for Missing Bolik), was quickly found and successfully completed the flight. Otvažnaya and Snezhinka: Otvažnaya (Brave One) flew on July 2, 1959, alongside a rabbit named Marfusha (Martha) and another dog, Snezhinka (Snowflake). Otvažnaya went on to complete five additional flights between 1959 and 1960. Albina and Tsyganka: Both dogs were ejected from their capsule at an altitude of 85 km and landed safely. Albina was shortlisted for the Sputnik 2 mission but never flew in orbit. Damka and Krasavka: These dogs were scheduled for an orbital flight on December 22, 1960, but the mission was aborted due to a rocket failure. They were recovered after an unplanned sub-orbital flight. Damka was also known as Shutka (Joke) and Zhemchuzhnaya (Pearly), while Krasavka was also called Kometka (Little Comet) and Zhulka (Cheater). Other dogs that participated in sub-orbital flights included Dymka (Smoky), Modnitsa (Fashionable), and Kozyavka (Little Gnat). At least four other dogs flew in September 1951, though two or more were lost. Orbital Flights Laika: Laika (Barker), originally named Kudryavka (Little Curly), became the first living Earth-born creature to orbit the Earth aboard Sputnik 2 on November 3, 1957. She died between five and seven hours into the flight due to stress and overheating. The true cause of her death was not revealed until 2002. Laika was also known as Zhuchka (Little Beetle) and Limonchik (Lemon). The American media nicknamed her Muttnik. The scientist responsible for the project later expressed regret for her death. Belka and Strelka: On August 19, 1960, Belka (Squirrel or Whitey) and Strelka (Little Arrow) spent a day in orbit aboard Korabl-Sputnik-2 (Sputnik 5) and returned safely. They were accompanied by a rabbit, 42 mice, 2 rats, flies, and various plants and fungi. Strelka later had six puppies, one of which, Pushinka (Fluffy), was gifted to President John F. Kennedy's daughter by Nikita Khrushchev. Pushinka's descendants are still alive today. Pchelka and Mushka: On December 1, 1960, Pchelka (Little Bee) and Mushka (Little Fly) spent a day in orbit aboard Korabl-Sputnik-3 (Sputnik 6). Their spacecraft disintegrated during re-entry due to a navigation error, and all aboard were killed. Mushka had been trained for Sputnik 2 but was excluded due to her refusal to eat properly. Chernushka: On March 9, 1961, Chernushka (Blackie) completed one orbit aboard Korabl-Sputnik-4 (Sputnik 9) with a cosmonaut dummy named Ivan Ivanovich, mice, and a guinea pig. The dummy was ejected during re-entry and landed safely, while Chernushka was recovered unharmed inside the capsule. Zvezdochka: Zvezdochka (Little Star), named by Yuri Gagarin, completed one orbit aboard Sputnik 10 on March 25, 1961, in the final test flight before Gagarin's historic mission. Both Zvezdochka and the dummy aboard were recovered safely. Veterok and Ugolyok: On February 22, 1966, Veterok (Little Wind/Breeze) and Ugolyok (Little Piece of Coal) were launched aboard Cosmos 110 and spent 22 days in orbit before landing on March 16. This record-breaking flight duration was not surpassed by humans until Skylab 2 in June 1973 and remains the longest spaceflight by dogs. The legacy of these space dogs is commemorated in various ways, including a photograph of their descendants displayed at the Zvezda Museum near Moscow.
